newsitem.title: USA: YEAREND -- U.S. labor markets seen tight in 1997.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND -- U.S. labor markets seen tight in 1997.

text.p: U.S. labor markets will likely remain tight in 1997 as enduring moderate economic growth keeps workers in high demand, economists and a former Federal Reserve official said.
"We're going to have a tight labor market next year," said Preston Martin, a former Fed vice-chairman and current chairman of Home Vest Financial Services Inc.
Wall Street analysts predict average monthly non-farm payroll gains will stay between 150,000 and 175,000 in 1997.
The unemployment rate, as estimated by the Economic Advisory Committee of PSA The Bond Market Trade Association, is seen averaging 5.3 percent next year.
The PSA Committee estimate represents a consensus forecast of 11 economists from major Wall Street and regional securities firms and banks.
Although labor markets are seen firm, analysts said the need for employees across various areas of the economy will be uneven.

Certain sectors, particularly ones that require a skilled, specialized workforce, are likely to have a hard time finding new personnel, analysts said. High-technology is one of the sectors most affected by the shortage of such workers.
Pundits say certain firms have been unable to find workers to perform specific functions such as computer security tasks.

The field of computer security is expected to expand quickly as the Internet grows into a more commerce-oriented network. Labor experts estimate that no more than 200 super computer security experts currently work in the U.S., and most, if not all, are not available for hire.
"The skills that are demanded for certain professionals ... are disproportionate to other things going on in the economy," said Richard Berner, chief economist at Mellon Bank.
This suggests that employers will have to either create training programs for new personnel or hire workers from other companies. Either way, experts say, wage-related costs are expected to rise.
Non-skilled labor is also seen tight in 1997, though in a much less intensive way.
Richard Rippe, chief economist at Prudential Securities Inc, detects some tightness even in the entry-level job market.
"Labor costs (in general) will rise a little bit in 1997," Rippe said.
What kind of impact can such a phenomenon have on the U.S. consumer inflation rate?

"I personally think you'll see inflation drift up a little bit (in 1997)," said William Dudley, chief U.S. economist at Goldman Sachs & Co. "But it's still a very gradual process. We don't have such a tight labor market that we're going to see inflation rising quickly."

Although some see a direct correlation between tight labor and inflation, most pundits say the unit labor cost, which measures employees' earnings against their productivity, is the indicator to watch.
"The problem is if you get rising wages and declining productivity growth," Dudley said. This might squeeze companies' costs and prompt some price hikes, he said.
Some analysts are also concerned about the possibility of a rise in consumption due to higher wages, which could ultimately put upward pressure on inflation.

"I think inflation will be more demand-driven (in 1997)," said Raymond Worseck, chief economist at A.G. Edwards & Sons. "I can see it happening in things that I buy. It's very slow, almost imperceptible, but I can start to see it.
"And I think that's what you should worry about, not that (firms) are going to raise prices."
Analysts interviewed by Reuters see, on average, productivity growth ranging from 1.0 to 1.3 percent in 1997.
Gross Domestic Product growth forecasts ranged from 2.1 to 2.3 percent.
